In this notebook you will explore accidents at work in Europe, using the European
Statistics on Accidents at Work (ESAW) published by Eurostat, the statistical office of the
European Union. Read the module [README](../README.md) and [data dictionary](../data_dictionary.md) first.

**How to use this notebook**

- Run each code chunk in order (the green arrow in RStudio, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter).
- Answer the questions under each **Your answer** heading.
- When you are done, click **Knit** to produce an HTML report to submit.

# Part 0. Load the data

The tables in `data/tidy/` are complete (not samples) and are committed to the repository.
To refresh them with the latest Eurostat data, run `scripts/fetch_data.R` and then
`scripts/build_dataset.R`.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)
library(forcats)

tidy_dir <- "../data/tidy"
github <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eddiekasner/occupational-safety-health-datasets/",
                 "main/modules/intl-eurostat-esaw/data/tidy")

read_tidy <- function(name, col_types = cols(year = col_integer(), value = col_double(),
                                              .default = col_character())) {
  local <- file.path(tidy_dir, name)
  read_csv(if (file.exists(local)) local else file.path(github, name), col_types = col_types)
}

main <- read_tidy("esaw_main.csv")
sector <- read_tidy("esaw_sector.csv")
causes <- read_tidy("esaw_causes.csv.gz")
codes <- read_tidy("esaw_codes.csv", col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))

fatal <- "Fatal"
nonfatal <- "Non-fatal (4+ days absence)"
```

# Part 1. Get oriented

ESAW counts accidents that cause **death** or **at least 4 calendar days of absence** from
work. Each table is in long format: one row per country, year, breakdown and `unit`.

```{r orient}
glimpse(main)
count(main, severity, unit)
count(main, flag)

# National totals: both sexes, all ages
totals <- main |> filter(sex == "T", age == "TOTAL")
latest_year <- max(totals$year)
cat("Years:", min(totals$year), "to", latest_year, "\n")
distinct(totals, country_code, country)
```

**Questions**

1. Which countries are included? Which European countries are missing, and why might the
   United Kingdom stop appearing after a certain year?
2. The `flag` column marks special values: `b` = break in time series, `e` = estimated,
   `u` = low reliability, `p` = provisional. Why does a break in series matter for trend analysis?

**Your answer:**



# Part 2. Fatal accidents by country

Eurostat publishes **standardised incidence rates**: accidents per 100,000 persons employed,
adjusted so that countries with more workers in high-risk sectors are not penalised
They cover NACE sections A and C to N (most of the business economy).

```{r fatal-countries, fig.height = 7}
fatal_latest <- totals |>
  filter(severity == fatal, unit == "standardised_incidence_rate", year == latest_year)

ggplot(fatal_latest, aes(value, fct_reorder(country, value),
                         fill = country_code == "EU27_2020")) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = paste("Standardised fatal accident rate,", latest_year),
       x = "Fatal accidents per 100,000 persons employed", y = NULL)
```

**Questions**

1. Which countries have the highest and lowest fatal rates? How many times higher is the highest?
2. Suggest two reasons, other than differences in workplace safety, that could explain the
   differences between countries.

**Your answer:**



# Part 3. Fatal versus non-fatal: a clue to under-reporting

Deaths are hard to leave unreported, but non-fatal accidents are not. If a country reports
very few non-fatal accidents for each death, many non-fatal accidents are probably missing.

```{r ratio, fig.height = 7}
ratio <- totals |>
  filter(unit == "standardised_incidence_rate", year == latest_year) |>
  select(country, severity, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = severity, values_from = value) |>
  filter(.data[[fatal]] > 0, .data[[nonfatal]] > 0) |>
  mutate(nonfatal_per_fatal = .data[[nonfatal]] / .data[[fatal]])

ggplot(ratio, aes(.data[[fatal]], .data[[nonfatal]], label = country)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text(size = 2.5, vjust = -0.6) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(title = paste("Fatal and non-fatal standardised accident rates,", latest_year),
       x = "Fatal per 100,000", y = "Non-fatal per 100,000 (log scale)")

arrange(ratio, nonfatal_per_fatal)
```

**Questions**

1. Which countries report the fewest non-fatal accidents per death? Which report the most?
2. Countries with the *lowest* non-fatal rates often have *high* fatal rates. What does that
   suggest? How might the type of reporting system (insurance-based vs. employer duty to
   report to a labour inspectorate) affect this?

**Your answer:**



# Part 4. Trends in the EU

```{r eu-trend}
totals |>
  filter(country_code == "EU27_2020", unit == "standardised_incidence_rate") |>
  ggplot(aes(year, value)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ severity, scales = "free_y") +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(title = "EU-27: standardised incidence rates of accidents at work",
       x = NULL, y = "Per 100,000 persons employed")
```

**Questions**

1. Describe the trends for fatal and non-fatal accidents.
2. What happened in 2020? Give two explanations (think about who was working, and where).

**Your answer:**



# Part 5. Who is injured? Age and sex

```{r age-sex}
eu_latest <- main |>
  filter(country_code == "EU27_2020", unit == "standardised_incidence_rate", year == latest_year)

eu_latest |>
  filter(sex == "T", age %in% c("Y_LT18", "Y18-24", "Y25-34", "Y35-44", "Y45-54", "Y55-64", "Y_GE65")) |>
  mutate(age = fct_relevel(age, "Y_LT18", "Y18-24", "Y25-34", "Y35-44", "Y45-54", "Y55-64", "Y_GE65")) |>
  ggplot(aes(age, value)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ severity, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = paste("EU-27 accident rates by age group,", latest_year), x = "Age", y = "Per 100,000")

eu_latest |>
  filter(age == "TOTAL", sex %in% c("F", "M")) |>
  select(sex, severity, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = severity, values_from = value)
```

**Questions**

1. How do fatal and non-fatal rates change with age? Why might young workers have more
   non-fatal accidents but older workers more fatal ones?
2. How many times higher is the fatal rate for men than for women? Is this mostly about sex,
   or about the jobs men and women do? How could you check?

**Your answer:**
